question: The European automotive industry, including the commercial vehicle sector, has for many months been raising the alarm about its deteriorating competitiveness vis-à-vis manufacturers from third countries.

Organisations representing manufacturers and social partners point to mounting problems arising from high energy prices, rising operating costs, the rapid pace of implementation of new climate and environmental regulations, and insufficiently developed infrastructure to support the sector’s transition.

At the same time, European manufacturers must compete with companies from outside the EU, which often operate under different regulatory and cost conditions. This is of particular concern for Poland, which is one of the EU’s largest manufacturers of buses, automotive parts and components, and a key link in European supply chains.
Tens of thousands of people are employed in this sector, and many companies are heavily dependent on the state of the wider European automotive market. In light of the foregoing: 1.

Has the Commission carried out an analysis of the impact of existing and planned climate and environmental regulations on the competitiveness of the European automotive industry, in particular on manufacturers and suppliers from Central and Eastern European countries, including Poland?
Does the Commission have data on the relocation of production, reduced investment or job cuts in the automotive sector which may be linked to costs arising from EU regulations?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (21.10.2026) The Commission is closely following restructuring and job cuts in the automotive sector. These developments are driven mainly by several structural factors: weaker demand in the EU, trade barriers in third countries, high energy and production costs, and growing competition from third-country manufacturers.

The Commission is aware that in Poland jobs have been lost at some vehicle manufacturers and suppliers, while at the same time many jobs and investments have been created by battery manufacturers and electric vehicles components suppliers. EU legislation1 has also given rise to business opportunities for the production of electric buses in Poland.
The Commission presented the Automotive Action Plan2 to support the sector’s competitiveness and resilience while accompanying the industrial transformation.

The recent Automotive Package3 and the Industrial Accelerator Act4 represent some of the most important follow-up actions, which aim to strengthen innovation, secure key supply chains, and create the right conditions for investment in Europe, including by reducing the administrative burden. All major Commission proposals for climate and environmental legislation are accompanied by an impact assessment.

The proposed Automotive Omnibus aims at further reducing the regulatory burden for vehicle manufacturers, inter alia by limiting Euro 7 type-approval emission testing for heavy-duty vehicles and relying more strongly on manufacturers’ declarations.
The Commission will continue to work with industry, Member States and social partners to help ensure that the transition remains fair, competitive and socially responsible.
